q186: Kavya and the panic on the flyover
q187: Kavya, 29, software tester in Bengaluru, drives to work every day
q188: It started on an ordinary Tuesday. Kavya was halfway up the long flyover near her office, stuck in slow traffic, when her heart began to pound. Her hands went cold on the steering wheel, her chest felt tight and she was sure she was about to faint or crash. She switched on her hazard lights and somehow reached the office, shaking. The doctor found nothing wrong with her heart. But the fear stayed. Soon she was taking long side roads to avoid the flyover, and then the panic began to show up in team meetings too. She started skipping the morning stand-up call, telling her manager the network was bad. At night she lay awake rehearsing escape routes. She felt foolish and weak, and she was ashamed to tell anyone at church.
q189: A panic attack is the body's alarm system firing at full volume when there is no real danger. The amygdala, a small alarm centre deep in the brain, picked up a mix of signals that morning: poor sleep, too much coffee, a tight deadline and the feeling of being trapped in traffic. It triggered the fight-or-flight response, flooding her body with adrenaline. Her heart raced and her breathing went fast and shallow, which made her dizzy and even more scared. Then avoidance taught her brain a lesson: the flyover is dangerous, escape keeps you safe. Each detour brought quick relief, which strengthened the fear loop. Kavya also carried an old belief from childhood that she must always look calm and capable.
q190: A friend from her cell group, a counsellor, explained that panic is like a wave. It rises, peaks and falls on its own, usually within minutes, if you do not fight it. Kavya realised her body was not broken. It was overprotecting her. That idea gave her courage to stop running and start practising.
q191: Learned the physiological sigh and practised it daily when calm, not only in panic
q192: Named the sensations aloud in the car, saying this is adrenaline and it will pass
q193: Built a fear ladder, starting with the flyover on a quiet Sunday with her sister beside her
q194: Used 5-4-3-2-1 grounding at red lights and before meetings
q195: Cut back from four coffees to one and protected her sleep
q196: Told her manager honestly and asked to keep her camera off for a few weeks
q197: Jesus slept in the boat while the storm raged, and when He woke He spoke peace to the wind and to His frightened friends (Mark 4:39-40). He did not shame them for being afraid. He drew near. Scripture often tells us not to fear, but it always gives a reason: I am with you (Isaiah 41:10). Kavya's healing was not about forcing herself to be brave by willpower. It was about learning, in her body, that God's presence goes with her onto the flyover. Paul says God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love and a sound mind (2 Timothy 1:7). Facing fear step by step, with God beside her, was a way of walking out that sound mind.
q198: God designed the alarm system to protect us. Without it, we would not jump back from a speeding bus. But He also gave us a brake. A long, slow breath out activates the vagus nerve, which tells the heart to slow down. Research suggests that slow exhale breathing can calm the body within a few minutes. God also designed the brain to keep learning. When we stay in a feared place long enough for the alarm to settle, the brain can update its map and file the place as safe. This is called graded exposure, and in studies it is one of the most effective approaches for panic. The same brain that learned fear can learn calm.
q199: Isaiah 41:10|Fear thou not, for I am with thee: be not dismayed, for I am thy God.
q203: After about three months Kavya could drive the flyover most days. She still felt a flutter in heavy traffic, and once she had a full panic attack after a sleepless week. This time she pulled over, breathed and waited, and it passed in six minutes. She no longer saw panic as a sign of danger or weak faith. She now leads a short session on anxiety in her cell group.
q204: Panic is a false alarm that loses its power when we stop running and let God walk with us through the wave.
